title: Connect an application to Nucleus
summary: Design and verify an application integration that uses Nucleus for constrained agent execution while keeping application data and success authority in the application.
use_when: A local application needs durable constrained agent execution through the shared Nucleus service.
An existing requester changes its invocation policy, immutable schemas, dynamic tools, identity, recovery, or compatibility boundary.
do_not_use_when: The current interactive agent can simply perform the requested work.
The proposed design requires Nucleus to understand requester domain rows or workflow state.
Only ordinary application code unrelated to the requester boundary is changing.
outcome: A requester with a defined external domain authority, one closed versioned invocation per job, durable correlation, idempotent tool handling, explicit failure policy, and proven operational recovery.
effects: Changes requester implementation, contracts, tests, and operator documentation.
May register new immutable decoder schemas or requester-owned toolset versions.
May change prompts, models, permissions, timeouts, deployment ordering, and retained job provenance.
authority: Nucleus owns portable invocation admission, harness supervision, authentication, job records, output atoms, and the tool mailbox.
The requester owns every domain mutation, domain success criterion, duplicate handling, and retry decision.
success: The requester proves strict health, admission, domain completion, duplicate handling, mailbox recovery, cancellation, timeout, daemon loss, and domain-success/runtime-failure distinctions.
No direct-runner fallback exists and retained historical jobs remain decodable.
The requester canary verifies the requester-owned authority rather than only Nucleus completion.
failure_and_recovery: Ambiguous admission retries only the byte-equivalent request under the same job ID.
A genuinely new attempt uses a new job ID and is allowed only by requester policy.
A requester restart may recover a durable pending call; a Nucleus restart cannot resume the Codex process and marks the attempt lost.
privacy: Treat both requester state and Nucleus output atoms according to all source, prompt, and tool-result content they may retain.
Document the working directory, workspace access, local execution, web search, launch context, and tool permissions explicitly.
steps: Run the installed Nucleus manual and define the requester-owned durable success condition before specifying a runtime request.
Choose the typed client or HTTP boundary, stable requester identity, job idempotency key, correlations, and complete invocation policy.
Version immutable schemas and tools, implement durable mailbox servicing, and separate domain success from terminal model prose.
Define failure and new-attempt policy, then add observability, security, backup, deployment, and canary coverage.
Update the requester and shared operator documentation whenever the integration boundary changes.
checkpoints: The requester domain authority and success proof are named and remain outside Nucleus.
Every invocation permission and immutable registration identity is explicit.
Duplicate admission and tool results are idempotent, and historical decoding is retained.
Requester and Nucleus restart semantics have separate tested recovery paths.
adaptation: Use the current installed manual and exact supported protocol rather than assuming source-workspace lockstep.
Change deployment order according to whether a public change is additive or incompatible.
stop_when: The domain result cannot be defined without making Nucleus understand application-specific state.
The required Nucleus protocol or harness capability is unsupported.
A destructive migration, credential move, or incompatible cutover lacks an explicit backup and recovery decision.
does_not_authorize: Domain changes outside the requester integration being developed.
Publishing a release or performing a production cutover.
